claims.claim: five whys done well, contributing-factor trees, separating trigger from cause, and actions that prevent the class of bug.
claims.note: Scope summary: Atlassian covers the five-whys method and branching into multiple factors, Cook covers contributing factors, and the SRE chapter covers blameless postmortems, but no fetched page covers contributing-factor trees, separating trigger from cause, or actions that prevent the class of bug.

claims.claim: Start from the precise failure and ask "why?" repeatedly
claims.evidence_quote: Identify the problem and ask why it happened. Then ask why that happened.
claims.note: The page continues: 'Then ask why that next thing happened. And so on until you get to the true root cause of your problem.'

claims.claim: each answer backed by evidence:
claims.note: The word 'evidence' appears zero times in the Atlassian 5-whys page and the SRE chapter; no readable source says each answer must be backed by evidence, and learningfromincidents.io was blocked from this environment today (SSL handshake failure on every attempt).

claims.claim: Why did customers get double-charged? The payment job ran twice for the same orders.
claims.note: Worked example: hypothetical double-charge scenario; no listed source documents it.

claims.claim: Why twice? Two workers picked the same batch.
claims.note: Worked example narrative; no listed source covers it.

claims.claim: Why? The batch lock expired while the first worker was still running.
claims.note: Worked example narrative (batch lock expiry); no listed source covers it.

claims.claim: Why? Lock TTL 60 s; the job took 4 min after the payment API slowed.
claims.note: Worked example numbers (60 s lock TTL, 4 min job); no listed source states these values.

claims.claim:
Why was that possible? The job wasn't idempotent and lock TTL wasn't tied to job duration
   (no lease renewal, no fencing).
claims.note: Worked example conclusion (idempotency, lease renewal, fencing); no listed source covers it.

claims.claim:
Fixes then target several levels: idempotency key per charge (prevents the class), lease renewal
with fencing tokens, alert on job duration, and API timeout.
claims.note: Fix list for the hypothetical scenario; no fetched page discusses idempotency keys, lease renewal with fencing tokens, or fixes at several levels.

claims.claim: most failures have **several contributing factors**; a single chain hides the others.
claims.evidence_quote: Because overt failure requires multiple faults, there is no isolated ‘cause’ of an accident. There are multiple contributors to accidents.
claims.note: Atlassian similarly: 'There’s no 5-whys police coming for you if your cause-and-effect chain turns into a tree of multiple factors.'

claims.claim: Draw a tree or fishbone (people/process/tooling/code/environment/dependencies).
claims.note: None of the three fetched pages mentions fishbone or Ishikawa diagrams or those cause categories; learningfromincidents.io was blocked today.

claims.claim: Stop at causes you can act on;
claims.evidence_quote: Five is shorthand for a process that pushes you to dig deeper until you hit the broken process or processes behind the incident.

claims.claim: don't stop at "human error".
claims.evidence_quote: Human error, team B’s screwup, and lack of employee X attention aren’t acceptable answers to the question.

claims.claim:
Ask why the system made the error
  easy and its consequences severe (Cook, How Complex Systems Fail).
claims.evidence_quote: Post-accident remedies for “human error” are usually predicated on obstructing activities that can “cause” accidents. These end-of-the-chain measures do little to reduce the likelihood of further accidents.
claims.note: The page names the essay and author (How Complex Systems Fail, Richard I. Cook, MD); the skill's phrasing distills Cook's argument that human-error attribution is hindsight-biased and end-of-chain remedies do little.

claims.claim:
Separate **trigger** (deploy, traffic spike, bad input) from underlying causes (missing
  validation, no rate limit).
claims.note: Neither Atlassian, the SRE chapter, nor Cook contrasts a trigger with underlying causes; learningfromincidents.io was blocked today so could not be checked.

claims.claim: Each "why" needs evidence (logs, code, metrics), not a guess.
claims.note: 'Evidence' appears zero times in the Atlassian 5-whys page and the SRE chapter; Cook's essay does not discuss evidence for whys either.

claims.claim:
Find the defect (the line), then ask why it was written, why review didn't catch it, why tests
  didn't, why monitoring didn't detect it sooner.
claims.note: The four-question chain for code bugs appears in none of the fetched pages; the sources cover incident postmortems, the 5-whys method and complex-system failure.

claims.claim: Each answer is a possible action.
claims.note: Method guidance; no fetched source states it.

claims.claim: Search for the **same pattern elsewhere** (`rg`, Semgrep/CodeQL query) and fix all instances.
claims.note: 'rg', 'Semgrep' and 'CodeQL' appear nowhere in the three fetched pages; no listed source documents searching for the same pattern or fixing all instances.

claims.claim: Add a regression test and, where possible, a static check that bans the pattern.
claims.note: None of the fetched pages mentions regression tests or static checks that ban a pattern.

claims.claim:
Summary, impact, timeline, root cause and contributing factors, what went well, action items with
owners and dates (prevent, detect, mitigate).
claims.note: Partial coverage only: the SRE chapter defines a postmortem as 'a written record of an incident, its impact, the actions taken to mitigate or resolve it, the root cause(s), and the follow-up actions to prevent the incident from recurring', and its blameless framing is confirmed, but 'timeline', 'what went well', 'owner' and 'date' appear nowhere in it.

claims.claim:
Track action items to completion; unfinished actions
are the most common postmortem failure.
claims.note: No fetched page says action items must be tracked to completion or that unfinished actions are the most common postmortem failure; the SRE chapter's closest text covers review sessions and a repository of past incidents.

coverage: I took the frontmatter description, the five-whys intro line and all five worked-example steps plus the fixes line (including the 60 s TTL and 4 min numbers), the four Rules bullets split into their component sentences, the three code-bug bullets and both write-up sentences, so that every number, tool name (rg, Semgrep/CodeQL) and behaviour is covered, and checked each against the three sources fetched today (https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/, https://www.atlassian.com/incident-management/postmortem/5-whys and https://how.complexsystems.fail/), while https://www.learningfromincidents.io/ rejected every fetch attempt today (web fetch tool, urllib with the attest user-agent and curl over https all failed with an SSL handshake failure, and http timed out), so only the fetched URLs appear in sources.
suggested_edits: Nothing is contradicted, but 17 of 22 claims are unverifiable against the sources that could be read. The Atlassian page confirms only the five-whys mechanics (identify the problem and ask why, digging to a broken process, human error not an acceptable answer), Cook's essay confirms only the multiple-contributors and end-of-the-chain-remedy points, and the SRE chapter confirms no claim in full - it defines a postmortem as a record of impact, root cause(s) and preventive actions but never mentions a timeline, 'what went well', owners or dates, nor tracking action items to completion; the fishbone categories, the trigger-vs-underlying-cause split, evidence for each why, the code-bug question chain, rg/Semgrep/CodeQL, the regression test and static-check guidance and the worked example are covered by no fetched page. A fix PR should bump version and cite sources that cover the missing material - an Ishikawa/fishbone diagram reference, the SRE Workbook's Postmortem Analysis chapter for the template list and action-item tracking, a page contrasting triggers with underlying causes and requiring evidence per why, and rg/Semgrep/CodeQL docs - or trim those sections to what the current sources support. Note also that https://www.learningfromincidents.io/ rejected every fetch from this environment today (SSL handshake failure over https, timeout over http), so re-fetch checks of that source will fail here.
